newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU's start to the grain year gets mixed reviews.
newsitem.headline: EU's start to the grain year gets mixed reviews.

text.p: European grain traders gave mixed reactions after the European Union kicked off a new grain campaign by granting 100,000 tonnes of wheat exports.

Some traders, supported by EU officials, said the sale was a gesture showing that Brussels wanted to have a presence in the market at the start of the July/June season, a different strategy from several previous years.
But critics were disappointed the Commission had not done more to satisfy "aggressive" demand at fob prices above $140 per tonne to close off unfinished business to Cuba and Iraq.
"I think it is a scandal to give 100,000 tonnes of soft wheat for two weeks," one trader said.
The EU usually holds grain export tenders each Thursday but is holding two meetings a month in July and August so the next auction will be on July 31.

Some traders had hoped the EU would respond to bids for refunds up to three or five Ecus per tonne, yielding fob French prices of $142 or $140 per tonne respectively. That would have allowed up to 238,000 tonnes of wheat onto the world market.
They said the modest volume given at some $144 a tonne failed to prove the EU was ready to start competing seriously with the United States at a time when soft red winter wheat is at $127 a tonne.
But one official familiar with EU policy said the award was a balanced indication that the EU was exporting. "It is a signal that we are in the market without going too far," he said.

The EU initially feared a spring drought could damage its crop and halted most exports in April. But it is now looking at another near-record crop of 200 million tonnes this year, which had raised industry hopes of a quick start to the campaign.

Traders said the wheat sale helped to plug short positions on outstanding sales to Cuba and Iraq. Some estimated the deficit at 150,000 to 200,000 tonnes but noted the size was impossible to confirm. "Who is going to show his cards now," commented one grain industry source.
Exporters, rarely equipped with glowing praise for the Commission which pays them subsidies, complained they would miss sales to North Africa because the EU was being too stingy.
Algeria, a traditional outlet for French wheat, is in the market for 75,000 tonnes of optional soft wheat.
"We are just out of it," one exporter said.
Rain in parts of northern Europe has also revived quality fears over the crop, meaning milling wheat is hard to secure with guarantees on quality in northern France just now.
Some also suggested exporters who still have to complete old wheat deals may turn to first come, first served "nil value" licences available through the EU's daily channel.
((-- Dominique Vidalon, Paule Bonjean, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5432))
